#Chapat_Ganesh
Chapat Ganesh is located around 500m east from Patan Durbar Square. The easiest way to get there is via Sundhara. When you reach Sundhara cross road, take a turn towards Northern narrower street (opposite side to the golden spout), keep on going straight then you will reach this place.

Chapat Ganesh has got a mythological story that quite amazes us. Normally, people of Patan visit this temple when they had lost something. There is a strong belief that, if someone looses something and offer Laddu to the Ganesh then they will find their lost objects.

That is why, Chapat Ganesh is regarded as one of the four main Vinayak established inside Patan city. It is the regarded as representation of Ashok Vinayak.

Mythology says, once Lord Shiva went to his trip to Maansarovar. Only Ganesh knew about his trip. All others were unknown. Even Nandi (Mahadev's vehicle, Basaaha) was unknown. Mischieviously, Ganesh sat on the Shiva's throne. When, Parvati came, she saw Ganesh sitting on Lord Shiva's place. Goddess Parvati asked Ganesh about Lord Shiva, he didn't say a word but kept smiling. She became worried and asked Nandi. He was unknown of the event either. The chaos came upon. Everyone became worried. They started searching here and there but they couldn't find him. Then there comes Ganesh's heroitic action. He said in loud voice, "Everyone don't worry. I will bring my lost father back." After that, he went Maansarovar and told all the story which had happened in the Kailash. Lord Shiva came back.
So it is said that the form of Ganesh which could even bring back Lord Shiva who was lost, how come he cannot bring back our lost objects.

That is why when we loose something we go there to offer Laddu or when we loose something, we take an oath, "If I find ........, I shall offer Laddu to Chapat Ganesh" and we find back the object, we have to offer laddu to that Ganesh.

By the above mythology it makes clear why there is an ox sitting infront of the Ganesh temple where there should have been an idol of Mouse.

Also there is a pond across a small street infront of this temple. In the middle of the pond there is an image of Lord Shiva, representing lord Shiva going to Maansarovar and in temple, Ganesh, sitting in the place of Lord Shiva.

The Nyatapola Temple is situated in Nepal’s Bhaktapur. This iconic building from the turn of the 18th century is the tallest temple in Nepal, rising to a height of more than 30 meters. The lovely brick and wood structure, resembling a pagoda, was dubbed Nyatapola, derived from the Newari terms for “roof” (pola) and “five-stepped” (nyata). It was lavishly carved.

Source: Atlas Obscura

Visiting the Nyatapola Temple in Bhaktapur's Durbar Square nearly two decades ago was an unforgettable experience. This towering five-storied pagoda, the tallest in Nepal, captivated me with its intricate carvings and sheer grandeur. Set within the enchanting Durbar Square, with its array of temples and palaces, the Nyatapola  stands out as a true architectural masterpiece. Even after all these years, I vividly remember the sense of awe and admiration I felt. It's a must-see destination for any visitor to Nepal.

The 55 Window Palace, also known as Pachpanna Jhyale Durbar in Nepali, is a historic palace located in Bhaktapur Durbar Square in Bhaktapur, Nepal. It was built during the reign of King Bhupatindra Malla in the 15th century and is considered one of the finest examples of traditional Newari architecture in Nepal.

The palace is named after its 55 intricately carved wooden windows, which are adorned with lattice work, statues of deities, and other decorative elements. The palace was originally used as a royal residence and a center for administration, and it was also the site of important ceremonies and events.

The 55 Window Palace is a three-story building with a central courtyard and a number of smaller rooms and chambers. The palace is built entirely from brick and timber, and its sloping roofs and ornate carvings are typical of Newari architecture. The palace is now a museum, where visitors can learn about the history of Bhaktapur and the Malla dynasty.

In addition to the 55 Window Palace, Bhaktapur Durbar Square is home to a number of other important structures, including the Golden Gate, the Taleju Temple, and the Natapole Temple, among others. The area is also known for its vibrant street life, with vendors selling traditional handicrafts, food, and other goods in the bustling squares and alleyways. Overall, Bhaktapur Durbar Square is a must-visit destination for anyone interested in Nepal's rich cultural heritage and history.

The 55 Window Palace (also known as Pachpanchhya Jhale) is a palace located in Bhaktapur Durbar Square, Nepal. It is a five-story palace with 55 intricately carved windows, hence the name. The palace was built in the 17th century by King Bhupatindra Malla and is considered one of the finest examples of Newari architecture.
The windows of the palace are made of sandalwood and are decorated with intricate carvings of flowers, animals, and other motifs. The palace also has a number of other features, including a courtyard, a water tank, and a library.
The 55 Window Palace was damaged in the 1934 earthquake, but it has since been restored. It is now a popular tourist destination and is one of the most photographed buildings in Bhaktapur.

A unique attraction in Aswan. Built by president Abdul Nasr in 1971 to control the floods from river Nile and for power generation. There is a view point where tourists are allowed to get down and enjoy the scenery after buying an entrance ticket. Both sides got magnificent views, one side the the Nasr lake and from the other side the river Nile.

The High Dam in Aswan is absolutely massive and really impressive to see in person. I couldn’t believe how huge it was and how much of an impact it’s had on Egypt. Standing on top of the dam, you really get a sense of how powerful and important it is for the region.

Our guide told us some really interesting stories about its construction and what it means for the country. It was built in the 1960s with help from the Soviet Union, and it’s incredible how it’s helped control the Nile River and provide electricity to so many people. The reservoir it created, Lake Nasser, is gigantic—it’s hard to wrap your head around the scale of it.

What stuck with me the most were the stories about how villages and even ancient monuments had to be moved because of the dam. It must’ve been such a huge project to pull off, and it’s amazing how they managed to preserve so much history while building something so modern. Definitely worth a visit if you're in Aswan and interested in these things.

Agnishala is an ancient and a sacred place for learning the rituals of fire. So called ‘Agni’, sanskrit word for fire and ‘shala’, sanskrit word for place of learning. This is the place where fire keeps on burning and no extra fuels are used while burning. Fire lighters and match sticks are strictly prohibited to generate fire. Fire is generated by the priests of the previous Agnihotri(Main priest elected by the descending order of age among the members). Same fire keeps on burning for the ages until the newly elected Agnihotri is alive. Papers, plastics, etc aren’t used, only woods and some special type of grains are used while burning, in Samskrit we call it as ‘hom’ or ‘hawan’.
Here in Agnishala there are 6 Yagyakunda. 1.BrahmaKunda, 2.RudraKunda, 3.VishnuKunda, 4.SuryaKunda, 5.NagKunda and 6.SabhyaKunda with 5 different types of fire; 1.Suryagni(Fire Generated from Sun), 2.Pasagni(from stone), 3.Kastagni(from wood), 4. Jalagni(from water) and 5.Garbhagni(from womb/abdomen of the female of Agnihotri). Top 5 Yagya Kundas are the kundas with the respective fire. And the Sabhya Kunda is not used generally. When Agnihotri dies, all the 5 kundas are destructurized, before doing so, fire from Vishnu Kunda is transferred to Sabhya Kunda and the rituals are performed in it until the selection of new Agnihotri. Before keeping the fire inside Sabhya kunda its called Asabhya Kunda and after the establishment of fire its called Sabhya Kunda. This transistional ritual is only performed by the Native Brahmins from Tädhalivi(near from Agnishala) until new Agnihotri is selected in Kartik. When new Agnihoti is selected, the whole former VishnuKunda complex is digger down until they find channel of running water(symbolic representation of the presence of river in that place in the ancient times), cover that water by jute, seed coat of rice, wooden dusts, etc and they built a new Vishnu Kunda, west to it Brahma Kunda, South west to VK, Rudra kunda and on the south-eastern corner there will be Surya Kunda. NagKunda and Sabhya kunda adjacent to Surya Kunda. In Bishnu Kunda and other, the former Agnihotri’s priests(Purohit) generate new fire. Till now the fire that is glowing is generated by Ghana Shyam Sharma from Tuelako/Mangalbazar when the Agnihotri from Patko, Nati-baje died in 2062-63(2007AD). Only the Native Brahmins of Lalitpur that have already finished Bratabandha ritual in his life and  are among 6origins(Kadkul)(Kul/Kawal)(Bakanimha, Mandichhen, Tadhalivi, Wolanimha, Swonimha and Nuga) and are members of Lalitpur Upakarma Guthi are allowed to go inside the Agnishala and perform thr rituals.

One of the four kumaris revered in the Kathmandu Valley is Balkumari of Madhyapur Thimi. She is revered by the locals as their protector deity. There, the natives hold rites for their daily lives including weddings and Barthabandha. A rectangular courtyard with brick pavers surrounds the Balkumari temple. Moreover, it contains both small and important deities, such as the Digu Bhairava shrine. The history of the temple is extensive and almost begins in the 17th century. Of sure, as it was the period the temple was built. According to folklore, a businessman from Madhyapur frequently traveled with his gang to Lubu for commercial purposes. But someway, both he and the princess of the Lubu, fell in love. The princess soon became pregnant as well. She requested that the merchant take her to the thimi as a result. The merchant gladly agreed to her proposition, but he also included a caveat. She had to bring the balkumari with her if she wanted to travel to Thimi with him. The princess did so with joy as well, bringing the deity to the thimi. The god was then permanently relocated to Thimi. Moreover, a womb-like structure is located directly above the deity's idol. This in some ways supports the myth about the pregnant women moving the deity.

Cultural preservation is crucial in this modern day world.

The Batsala Temple is the shikhara style temple, which was built by King Jagat Prakash Malla and is similar to the Krishna Temple in Patan. In the
front of the temple is a large Taleju Bell erected by King Ranajit Malla in 1737.

Sadly the temple was completely destroyed in the April 25th earthquake in Nepal. It is currently it is restored (2020). Several smaller monuments have been rebuilt near it. The Vatsala Durga Temple is made from sandstone and sits beside King Bhupatindra Malla's statue directly in front of the Royal Palace of 55 Windows. Though sandstone its appearence is more of limestone. The Taleju Bell was placed there to mark morning and evening prayers at the Taleju Temple and is undamaged. Visited this temple back in 2012 before the devastating Gorkha earthquake flattened this beautiful Shikhara style temple. This temple was constructed in sandstone and is built upon a three-stage plinth. The bell in front of the temple is the Telaju Bell, or the bell of barking dogs. Apparently when it was rung every morning when goddess Taleju was worshiped, the dogs will barked and howled. Mysteriously, this bell survived the 2015 earthquake.

This stone temple is without doubt a smaller version of the Patan Krishna mandir. It has three steppen base. The colonnade has fourteen octagonal pillars like the Patan temple. There is no upper storey, but there are eight features above the cornice; at the corners are octagonal turrets, in the form of miniature temples, and four small pavilions are set on the faces of the Shikhara. The structure is completed by a tapering Shikhara and a finial with two bell-shaped members, amalakas, kalasha, and a trident. The temple was built by Bhupatindra Malla in the late seventeenth or early eighteenth century and consecrated to Batsala Devi. She is probably a form of Durga as the goddess in the pavilion above the main door and the image of as eighteen-armed Mahishamardini located inside the sanctum door suggest. - Kathmandu Valley Inventory

The colossal bell was hung by King Ranjit Malla in 1737 AD and was used to sound the daily curfew. It was rung every morning when goddess Taleju was worshiped. Despite the Temple being completely demolished by the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, the bell remains intact.

Nestled in the serene hills of Palpa, Bhairabsthan Temple stands as a revered religious site with deep historical and cultural significance located about 10 km north west from the city of Tansen, in Palpa district of Nepal at an elevation of about 1470 m. Hindu people worship at the temple mainly in Mahaastami of Dashain. During the festivals, animal sacrifices (buffalo, goat, sheep and rooster) are performed in the temple. Pancha Bali is also performed, which involves the sacrifice of five kinds of animals namely buffalo, goat, sheep, rooster and duck. The temple is famous for the iconic trident which is considered as the biggest in Nepal. Dedicated to Bhairab, a fearsome incarnation of Lord Shiva, the temple is an important pilgrimage destination for devotees and visitors alike, offering both spiritual solace and a panoramic view of the surrounding landscape.
The temple is also surrounded by dense forests, adding to its tranquil atmosphere. As you approach the temple, the view of the surrounding valleys, rivers, and distant snow-capped mountains makes for a perfect backdrop, allowing visitors to immerse themselves in both natural beauty and spirituality.
Devotees visit to seek blessings for protection, strength, and the removal of obstacles in their lives. It is believed that Lord Bhairab, known for his wrathful nature, helps to drive away evil forces and ensures the safety and well-being of his devotees.
One of the most remarkable features of the Bhairabsthan Temple is the stunning panoramic view from the temple’s premises. From the top of the hill, you can enjoy breathtaking views of Palpa’s valleys, the Kali Gandaki River, and even distant snow-capped peaks. The temple is particularly beautiful at sunrise and sunset when the light casts a golden glow over the landscape, making it a perfect spot for photography and reflection.

Bhairabsthan Temple is more than just a place of worship; it is a serene retreat that offers visitors a glimpse into the spiritual and cultural heart of Nepal. Kal Bhairab Temple (Bhairabsthan) is one of the biggest hindu temple of lord Kal Bhairab (Bhairav) . The main days for worshiping this temple is Tuesdays and Saturdays. Beside that many pilgrims come to visit this temple in the month of Mangsir (Nov-Dec). The busiest day of the temple is on the day of Maha Ashtami of Navaratra.

The main parsad of this temple is "Rot", which is made up of wheat flour. "Rot" is a secret rice bread that can be eaten after it has been worshiped in the temple. Different kind of animal sacrifice called "Pancha Bali" (five animal sacrifice is also done in this temple.)

Literally Pancha Bali Means Sacrifice of five kinds of animals, buffalo, goat, sheep, hen and duck. Only the males of these animals can be sacrificed in the shrines of gods and goddesses. After the fulfillment of the wish, a day is fixed for Pancha Bali, according to lunar calendar. Generally the eight-day of the new moon or full moon day is preferred.

To offer Pancha Bali people go to the temple from their house in processions. A music band called Pancha Baja of local musicians heads the procession. At the temple the god or goddess is worshipped ceremoniously and the animals and bird are sacrificed one by one. Generally the buffalo is given to the members of the musical band.

Since the temple is on the top of the hill, you can see the beautiful range of Mt. Machhapuchhre, Mt. Annapurna and Mt. Dhaulagiri.

Bhalupahad, located in Syangja district, Nepal, is a picturesque region nestled amidst the breathtaking landscapes of the Himalayas. Characterized by its lush greenery, terraced fields, and traditional Nepalese architecture, Bhalupahad is a tranquil haven that captivates visitors with its natural beauty.

The village is surrounded by majestic mountains, providing a stunning backdrop to everyday life. The locals, predominantly engaged in agriculture, cultivate terraced fields that cascade down the hillsides, creating a mesmerizing patchwork of vibrant greenery. The agricultural practices are deeply rooted in the region's culture, and the terraces not only serve as a means of sustenance but also contribute to the area's scenic allure.

Bhalupahad is known for its warm and welcoming community, where traditions and customs are preserved with great pride. The village is home to various ethnic groups, each adding to the rich cultural tapestry of the region. Traditional festivals, dances, and rituals are integral to the community's social fabric, offering visitors a unique insight into the local way of life.

The surrounding natural environment provides ample opportunities for outdoor enthusiasts. Hiking trails meander through the hills, offering panoramic views of the Himalayan peaks and the lush valleys below. Bhalupahad also serves as a gateway to explore the diverse flora and fauna of the region, making it a destination not only for cultural enthusiasts but also for nature lovers.

In recent years, efforts have been made to promote sustainable tourism in Bhalupahad, aiming to preserve its pristine environment and promote responsible travel. As a result, visitors can experience the beauty of this Himalayan gem while contributing to the well-being of the local community and the preservation of its unique heritage. Bhalupahad stands as a testament to the harmonious coexistence of nature and culture in the heart of the Himalayas.

Bhandarkhal Pokhari, situated near Mangal Bazar in Patan, is a historic pond that carries immense cultural and historical significance. Once part of the Patan Durbar Square complex, this serene water reservoir is an excellent example of traditional Newar engineering and water management systems.

The pond was historically used for religious rituals, royal ceremonies, and community purposes, making it an integral part of local life. Surrounded by lush greenery and traditional architecture, Bhandarkhal Pokhari provides a tranquil escape amidst the bustling streets of Mangal Bazar. Its proximity to the iconic Patan Durbar Square further adds to its importance as a cultural heritage site.

Recently restored to preserve its legacy, the pond showcases traditional craftsmanship, with its stone-paved embankments and intricate spouts reflecting the Newar community's architectural brilliance. It also plays a significant role in maintaining the area's ecological balance, serving as a rainwater harvesting system.

Visitors to Bhandarkhal Pokhari can experience a blend of history and nature, making it a perfect spot for reflection and relaxation. Bhundol Ground, located in the Lalitpur district of Nepal, is a popular and vibrant open space that serves as a hub for sports and community activities. Nestled within the urban environment of Patan, Bhundol Ground has become an integral part of the local community, providing a much-needed recreational area amidst the densely populated cityscape.

The ground is best known for hosting a variety of sports, particularly football and cricket. On any given day, one can find local youth engaged in spirited matches, honing their skills, and fostering a sense of camaraderie. The ground also serves as a venue for various sports tournaments, bringing together teams from different neighborhoods and even from across the city. These events often draw crowds of enthusiastic spectators, adding to the lively atmosphere.

In addition to sports, Bhundol Ground is a venue for cultural events, festivals, and social gatherings. During major festivals like Dashain and Tihar, the ground becomes a focal point for community celebrations, with temporary stages set up for performances, games, and other festive activities. It’s also a space where local fairs and markets occasionally take place, contributing to the economic activity of the area.

Beyond its role in sports and events, Bhundol Ground is a vital green space in the urban setting of Patan, providing residents with a place to relax, exercise, and enjoy the outdoors. It embodies the spirit of community in Lalitpur, serving as a gathering place that fosters social interaction, physical activity, and cultural expression.

Bikram Baba is a serene and peaceful religious place located inside the Chitwan National Park. It's an ideal place for those who seek a spiritual connection with nature and want to escape from the hustle and bustle of the city.

The moment you enter Bikram Baba, you can feel a sense of tranquility and calmness that is hard to find in other places. The peaceful atmosphere, surrounded by the lush greenery of the national park, creates an aura of spiritualism that is truly divine.

Overall, Bikram Baba is a hidden gem inside the Chitwan National Park, and it's definitely worth a visit for those who seek spiritual solace in nature. The beauty and tranquility of this place will leave you feeling refreshed and rejuvenated.

Bikram Baba is a popular religious place at Kasara. Kasara is the headquarters of "Chitwan national park" which is one of the world heritage sites (designated by UNESCO) of Nepal. Bikram Baba, a revered spiritual person, considered like a god, had been worshipped by some local communities, especially by some native communities (Tharu, Darai, etc.), residing near the park area for a long time. Over the time many people in Jagatpur and Patihani, the places on the lap of Chitwan national park, started worshipping Bikram Baba, and gradually Bikram Baba became one of the major cultural figures, and the place where people established a sort of monument became one of the major tourist attractions. The popularity of the place is mainly due to its location: people, during their visit to Bikram Baba, can enjoy the park’s green forest, tranquil Rapti river and the aquatic lives in the river clearly visible from a landmark bridge, some unexpected encounters of wildlife, a world class crocodile breeding center, Kasara museum, palaces built by ancient rulers, an awesome site of an army force unit, etc. In general, one can go and visit Bikram Baba at any time, but a large flow of domestic tourists to the place, which takes a form of so-called “MELAA”, takes place during 15 days of lunar phase from a new moon to the next full moon of “Chaitra” (March-April).

One of the most intriguing features of Buda Subba Temple is its connection to local legends. According to folklore, Buda Subba was a Kirati king who once ruled the area, and it is believed that the temple is located on his burial ground. A defining element of the temple is the grove of bamboo stalks with blunt tips. It’s said that no bamboo here grows with pointed ends, which adds an element of mystery and reverence. Locals believe this phenomenon is a blessing from the spirit of Buda Subba, and many people come to the temple to make wishes by tying threads around the bamboo stalks, hoping for prosperity, health, and happiness.

Budha Subba Temple: A Cultural and Spiritual Landmark in Eastern Nepal

Located in the picturesque town of Bijayapur, Dharan, Nepal, the Budha Subba Temple is a revered and culturally significant site that attracts devotees from various backgrounds. This temple, nestled in the eastern region of Nepal, is steeped in history, mythology, and unique traditions that set it apart from other religious sites.

Location and Accessibility

The temple is situated on top of Bijayapur Hill, overlooking the Seuti River, and is approximately 220 km away from Kathmandu. Its geographic coordinates are 26.820°N 87.30°E, making it easily accessible for both local and international visitors.

Historical Significance

The Budha Subba Temple is primarily known as the tomb of King Buddhi Karnaraya Khebang, the last Limbu King of Morang. King Buddhi Karnaraya Khebang was assassinated by the assassins of King Prithvi Narayan Shah of the Kingdom of Nepal during negotiations in Bijayapur-Dharan. Despite the tragic circumstances of his death, the locals have transformed this site into a place of reverence, worshiping the king's spirit as a friendly and helpful presence believed to bring good luck.

Unique Features and Worship Practices

One of the striking features of the Budha Subba Temple is the absence of an idol, a departure from the conventional setup of many religious sites. Instead, devotees worship two earthen bases within the ancient temple, revered as Budha Subba and Budhi Subban. This unconventional aspect adds an air of mystery and uniqueness to the temple.The temple complex is also notable for its tip-less bamboo plants, a phenomenon attributed to the legend of Budha Subba. According to myth, Budha Subba, a hunter, accidentally broke the tips of the bamboo trees while hunting crows, and they never grew back.

Rituals and Offerings

Devotees flock to the temple, especially on Saturdays, to partake in rituals that involve the sacrificial offerings of animals such as pigs and chickens. These offerings are seen as gestures of devotion and expressions of gratitude to the deity, believed to have the power to fulfill wishes and bring good fortune.

Cultural and Mythological Significance

The temple is surrounded by numerous myths and legends. One legend connects the temple to Eklavya, a character from the Mahabharata, who is said to have meditated at this site. Another myth involves Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati, who allegedly arrived at Vijaypur in disguise and performed penance, leading to the bamboo sprouting without tips.The temple also holds significance for young couples, who believe that tying colorful strings around the bamboo trees and engraving their names will bring them happiness and long life together.

Atmosphere and Facilities

The temple complex offers a peaceful and meditative environment, ideal for those seeking spiritual solace. The surroundings are tranquil, and the absence of an idol creates a unique and inclusive atmosphere that attracts devotees from various religious backgrounds. The temple also features a small car parking facility and souvenir shops within the complex.

Conclusion

The Budha Subba Temple is more than just a religious site; it is a repository of history, mythology, and cultural traditions. Its unique features, diverse legends, and inclusive atmosphere make it a fascinating destination for those seeking spiritual solace and a deeper connection to the rich cultural heritage of eastern Nepal. Whether you are a local or an international visitor, the Budha Subba Temple is a must-visit site that offers a profound and enriching experience.

Budha Subba Temple stands as a revered religious site among the Nepali community, gracing the landscape of Bijayapur in Dharan, Nepal. This sacred sanctuary is renowned for its perceived ability to fulfill the wishes of its visitors and bestow good fortune upon them. According to Kirat historian Iman Singh Chemjong, Bijayapur once served as the capital of the Limbuwan Kingdom under the rule of King Bijayanarayan Raya Khebang. Alternatively, some accounts attribute the name Bijayapur to King Bijaya.

Steeped in history, the temple is considered the final resting place of the last Limbu King, Budhhi Karna Khebang of Limbuwan (Pallo Kirat). Tragically, he was lured to Bijaypur-Dharan for negotiations in 1773, only to fall victim to the assassins of Gurkhali King Prithvi Narayan Shah of the Kingdom of Nepal. Legend has it that Budhhi Karna Khebang's benevolent spirit roamed the vicinity of his tomb, inspiring local Limbu inhabitants to venerate him as an ancient king (Hang signifies King in Limbu language) believed to bring blessings and good fortune.

Bulbule Lake in Surkhet District, Nepal, is a captivating destination that offers a blend of natural beauty and recreational activities. Located in Birendranagar, this lake is renowned for its unique feature where water bubbles up from a natural spring, giving it its name.

The lake is situated within Bulbule Park, a beautifully maintained public park that provides a serene environment for visitors. The park is adorned with a variety of flowers, including roses and other imported species, and lush green lawns that make it an ideal spot for picnics and leisurely walks2. The park’s cleanliness and well-organized layout enhance the overall experience, making it a favorite among locals and tourists alike.

One of the main attractions of Bulbule Lake is its crystal-clear water, which is home to various fish and other aquatic life. The lake’s natural beauty is complemented by the surrounding landscape, which includes scenic views and tranquil spots perfect for relaxation and meditation. The park also offers boating and fishing activities, adding to the recreational options available to visitors.

Bulbule Lake is not just a place of natural beauty but also holds cultural significance. It has inspired many poets and musicians, and the popular Nepali song “Surkhetma Bulbule Taal” is a testament to its charm. The lake and its surroundings are often used for cultural rituals and community events, making it a vibrant part of the local culture.

Bulbule Lake is a must-visit destination in Surkhet District. Its unique bubbling spring, beautiful park, and range of activities make it a perfect spot for a day out with family or friends. Manimukunda Sen Park, located near Butwal in the Rupandehi District of Nepal, is a picturesque and historically significant park. Named after King Manimukunda Sen, a medieval king of the Palpa kingdom, it is easily accessible by road, making it a convenient day trip for visitors staying in Lumbini. The park is renowned for its lush greenery, well-maintained gardens, and peaceful ambiance and is a popular spot for picnics and family outings.

According to local legends, the king used the area as a summer retreat. The ruins of his palace can still be seen within the park, adding a historical dimension to the natural beauty of the area. Visitors can enjoy leisurely walks along tree-lined paths, relax on well-manicured lawns, and take in the scenic views of the surrounding hills. It also features a variety of plant species, making it a haven for botany enthusiasts. The park includes a designated play area for children, equipped with swings, slides, and other playground equipment.

Manimukunda Sen Park, located in Butwal, Nepal, is a historic and scenic park that serves as a significant cultural and recreational spot. Named after King Manimukunda Sen, a 16th-century ruler of the Palpa Kingdom, the park is known for its lush greenery, ancient artifacts, and panoramic views of the surrounding area. The park is situated on the banks of the Tinau River and offers a peaceful environment for visitors, with beautifully landscaped gardens, walking trails, and picnic spots.

One of the park's main attractions is the ruins of the palace of King Manimukunda Sen, which offer a glimpse into the region's rich history. The site is also popular among locals and tourists for its religious significance, as it is near the historic temple of Siddhababa, making it a place of both cultural and spiritual importance. Visitors often enjoy the tranquil atmosphere and the opportunity to explore the remnants of Nepal's medieval history in this serene setting.

The Butwal View Point is a popular spot located in the Rupandehi district of Nepal, offering breathtaking panoramic views of the surrounding landscapes. It is one of the key attractions near Butwal for both locals and visitors seeking a peaceful escape and stunning vistas.

Key Features of Butwal View Point:

1. Scenic Beauty: The viewpoint provides a bird's-eye view of Butwal city, the Terai plains, and even the foothills of the Chure range.

2. Accessibility: Located a short drive from Butwal city, the site is easily reachable by road, making it a convenient destination.

3. Peaceful Atmosphere: The area is quiet and serene, ideal for relaxation or a short day trip.

4. Photography: A great spot for capturing sunsets, city lights, and scenic landscapes.

Nearby Attractions:

Siddhababa Temple: A spiritual and religious site on the Siddhartha Highway.

Manimukunda Park (Phulbari): A historical and recreational park in Butwal.

Bat cave which is known as Chamero Gufa in the Nepali language was discovered by the local people of the area in 2043 B.S. (1986 A.D.). The cave is home to thousands of bats of different species and therefore, is known as a Bat cave. It is located around 10 kilometers northwest of Lakeside Pokhara in Pokhara Metropolitan City Ward No. 16. A 10-minute walk from Mahendra Cave will take you to the gates of this mind-blowing cave.

Surprisingly, This cave was on private land during the time of its discovery. Later, Bindhyabasini secondary school took ownership of the land and its management.

Once you go inside the cave, you will reach a huge space. The cave is built from Limestone and is a habitat for different species of bats. You will be able to notice them hanging upside down at the walls, corners, and ceilings of the cave with the help of an emergency light provided by the counter. The different species of bats found in this cave feed on fruits and insects. The cave is 225 meters long and there are two different entry and exit routes

One of the major attractions in Pokhara is the stunning Bat Cave, an incredible natural wonder. Inside the cave, you’ll have the unique opportunity to see live bats hanging from the ceiling. The narrow pathways leading through the cave can be challenging, requiring careful navigation, but this only enhances the thrill of exploration. I highly recommend to visit with a local guide.
Overall, Bat Cave is a must-visit destination for anyone traveling to Pokhara, offering a perfect blend of natural beauty and adventure.

Nestled in the heart of Banepa, about 25 kilometers east of Kathmandu, lies the Chandeshwori Temple, locally known as Chasa: Ajima. This temple is a significant cultural and religious site in Nepal, dedicated to the goddess Chandeshwori, an avatar of the Hindu goddess Durga.

Believed to have been built in the 17th century, the Chandeshwori Temple features a stunning three-tiered pagoda-style architecture. One of its most remarkable aspects is the mural depicting Chandeshwori slaying the demon Chanda, a testament to its rich mythological heritage.

Chandeshwari is the avatar taken by Hindu goddess Kumari of Hindu. The 'Nepal Mahatmya' of Skanda Purana mentions the story related to goddess Chandeshwari.
Along Arniko Highway 5 kilometers before Dhulikhel is the town of Banepa, Nepal. One of the attractions of Banepa is the temple of Chandeshwori, located approximately 1 kilometer northeast of the town along the Punya mata River next to Ghokechaur having a length of 0.21 kilometres.

It is believed to have been built in the 17th century. The temple features a mural of Chandeshwori slaying the demon Chanda. The temple also consists of the painting of lord Bhairava on one of its wall which is the biggest graffiti of the Nepal Mandala.

Myth

edit

There is myth that the Chandeshwori temple is the place where the mother goddess (Sati / Parvati and in Banepa known as Chandeshwori) defeated the demon Chanda. The demon was a plague to the world since Shiva gave him a boon that made him unbeatable except by women. The desperate gods asked Brahma for advice and he sent them to the forest around Banepa where the mother gods lived in those days. In the meantime, Narada went to Chanda and provoked him to come to Banepa to fight the gods. When Chanda arrived with a big army of demons, all the gods took the forms of different birds and flew. The mother goddess quickly disappeared in a tree but Chanda saw that and cut down the tree with his sword. Now the goddess appeared on a big lion and a terrible fight between her and Chanda started. But Chanda had no chance and was killed by the mother goddess. Out of the belly of Chanda who was a big devotee of Shiva a lingam grew. This lingam can be seen in the small temple just in front of the big temple in the Chandeshwori temple complex. It is said that down at the big rocks around the river you can still see the marks of the big fight between the goddess and the demon.

The Chhabdi Barahi Temple is located in Chhabdi Barahi Village, Tanahun District. It is the source of the Chhabdi River, which flows from a small pond in the temple compound. It is believed that Satyavati was born here in the form of a fish, and fishes play an important role in the cultural traditions of the temple. Death rites in keeping with Hindu traditions are performed for fishes that die here, with the priest playing the role of the son of the fish.

Along with that of Satyavati there are idols of many different gods and goddesses in the temple compound, including a temple of Bhimsen. Dozens of goats are sacrificed to Barahi every month. However, no animal sacrifice takes place during Aunsi, Ekadashi, and the month of Shrawan. It is also believed that menstruating women and their husbands should not visit the temple.

Chhabdi Barahi Temple (Mandir) is a holy temple situated in a hilly forest located in Tanahun district of western Nepal. It is said that Chhabdi Barahi and Dhor Barahi temples are sisters and both are religious temples according to Hindu mythology. The temple is dedicated to Fish Headed Goddess, which is known about two hundred years ago. Before the existence of the temple, the local people over there go fishing to this site and one day a fired arrow to fish mistakenly stuck in the rock and suddenly blood appears on it. After this incident, fishing was stopped to this site, instead, a small shrine was constructed to this site which is well known as Chhabdi Barahi Temple in these days.

Chitwan National Park, located in south-central Nepal, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site renowned for its rich biodiversity and stunning landscapes. Established in 1973 as the country's first national park, it spans 932 square kilometers and encompasses dense forests, grasslands, rivers, and wetlands. The park is home to an impressive array of wildlife, including the endangered one-horned rhinoceros, Bengal tiger, Asian elephant, and gharial crocodile. It is also a haven for birdwatchers, with over 500 species of birds recorded. Visitors can enjoy activities such as jungle safaris, canoeing, birdwatching, and cultural interactions with the indigenous Tharu community. Chitwan National Park offers a unique blend of natural beauty, wildlife conservation, and cultural heritage, making it a must-visit destination in Nepal.

Cholung Park: Explore Nature, Embrace Heritage!

Cholung Park, located in Terathum's Laligurans Municipality, is a hidden gem that beautifully blends cultural heritage with natural beauty. Known for its breathtaking views and vibrant rhododendron blooms, the park is especially popular during peak flowering season in March. It's an essential stop for anyone interested in the rich traditions of the indigenous Limbu community and offers an immersive experience into their history and spiritual beliefs.

The park's highlight is the mysterious "lung" stone pillars, thought to have been erected for rituals, grave markers, and to resolve clan disputes. These stones, alongside the sacred Cholung Worok Pond, embody the deep connection the Limbu people have with nature. Visitors can also explore ancient cultural artifacts, including sacred beads, weapons, and historical documents housed in the Yuma Museum.

Cholung Park also shines as a model for ecological conservation, with over 150 plant species, including medicinal herbs and various rhododendron species. The park provides a peaceful, educational experience with its traditional village square, nature trails, and cultural exhibits, all of which showcase the Limbu community's bond with their ancestors and environment.

If you're looking to learn about indigenous culture, explore stunning nature, or enjoy peaceful walks surrounded by breathtaking views, Cholung Park is a must-visit destination. Don't forget to capture the beautiful scenery for your photos!

Highlights:
- Stunning views with vibrant rhododendron blooms.
- Rich cultural and historical significance, showcasing Limbu traditions.
- The Yuma Museum with historical artifacts, including fossils and ancient documents.
- Sacred stone pillars ("lung") and a traditional Limbu village square.
- More than 150 species of plants, including medicinal herbs and rhododendron varieties.
- A peaceful spot for nature lovers and cultural enthusiasts alike.

Recommendations;
- Best time to visit: March for the rhododendron bloom.
- Ideal for photography, history buffs, and nature lovers.

Chyasilin Mandap, a part of Bhaktapur Durbar Square and its heritage

Chyasilin Mandap literally means an octagonal pavilion in the local Newari language. Unfortunately for this pavilion, it's artistic wooden struts are being used to decorate the New Road Gate in Kathmandu, and plain wooden strut is in use in the pavilion. Hopefully, this octagonal pavilion gets back it's artistic struts.

This Chyasin Mandap was completely destroyed in the earthquake of 1934 A.D. The present structure was reconstructed in 1989 A.D., with
the assistance of the German Government. It was reconstructed to commemorate the visit of Chancellor Helmut Kohl to Bhaktapur: Poke your head inside and note the earthquake resistant steel-beams on the
lower level. There has been much controversy over their construction. Local craftsmen complained that these beams destroyed the ritual efficacy of the Mandap because the use of metal in temple construction is ritually prohibited, and that they should at least be covered in wood.

And it is rumored that the American First Lady Hillary Clinton, when she was given a tour of the site also questioned their aesthetic value.

Located on the eastern side of Bhaktapur Durbar square Chyasain Mandap is a small two storied wooden pavilion immediately opposite the Palace of 55 Windows was probably used by Bhaktapur's kings to watch festivals and processions.

Dhaulagiri I is known as the White Mountain is the seventh highest peak in the world. This peak is very popular among the eight-thousanders for expeditions. It lies northwest of Pokhara, an important tourist center. When Dhaulagiri I was discovered in 1808, it was thought to be the highest mountain peak in the world.

The Dhaulagiri massif in Nepal extends 120 km (70 mi) from the Kaligandaki Riverwest to the Bheri. This massif is bounded on the north and southwest by tributaries of the Bheri River and on the southeast by Myagdi Khola. Dhaulagiri I is the seventh highest mountain in the world at 8,167 metres (26,795 ft) above sea level, and the highest mountain within the borders of a single country (Nepal). It was first climbed on May 13, 1960 by a Swiss/Austrian/Nepali expedition.
The mountain's name is धौलागिरी (dhaulāgirī) in Nepali. This comes from Sanskrit where धवल (dhawala) means dazzling, white, beautiful[3]and गिरि (giri) means mountain.[4] Dhaulagiri I is also the highest point of the Gandaki river basin.

Annapurna I (8,091m/26,545 ft) is 34 km. east of Dhaulagiri I. The Kali Gandaki River flows between the two in the Kaligandaki Gorge, said to be the world's deepest.[citation needed]The town of Pokhara is south of the Annapurnas, an important regional center and the gateway for climbers and trekkers visiting both ranges as well as a tourist destination in its own right.

Dhulabari Chowk, located in the picturesque municipality of Jhapa District, Nepal, stands as a bustling crossroad junction and a pivotal point on the East-West Highway. Let me try to give some insights into the various facets of this marketplace and its significance in the region.

Geographical Significance:
Situated in the southeastern part of Nepal near the Indian border, Dhulabari serves as a strategic transit point for travelers journeying between Nepal and India. With a population of around 50,000, it is a vibrant hub connecting major cities, making it an essential stop for those traversing the East-West Highway.

Marketplace Dynamics:
Dhulabari boasts a diverse marketplace that, despite its size, offers a variety of shops, cafes, and amenities. Noteworthy is the Chinese market, established in 1977, renowned for providing a wide array of Chinese goods. While the market is relatively small, its charm lies in the availability of foreign-made products, making it a unique destination for shoppers.

Infrastructure and Services:
The marketplace features essential services such as banks, insurance, ATMs, and emergency facilities like hospitals, ensuring the well-being and convenience of residents and visitors. However, it is also important to highlight concerns about road maintenance, noting that the existing roads, though good, might need attention, especially given the size of the bustling marketplace.

Proximity to Major Cities:
Dhulabari's advantageous location near major cities like Kakarvitta, Birtamod, and Bhadrapur enhances its appeal. Being only 6 km east of Kakarvitta, which marks the international border with India along the Mechi River, further solidifies its significance in the region.

Connectivity and Accessibility:
The municipality is well-connected to all parts of Nepal through the Mahendra Highway, fostering accessibility for both local residents and travelers. Additionally, the Chandragadhi Airport, located approximately 16 kilometers away, provides convenient air travel options, with frequent flights to and from Kathmandu.

Thus, Dhulabari Chowk is not merely a crossroad junction but a dynamic marketplace woven into the fabric of the region. Its cultural richness, strategic location, and diverse offerings make it a noteworthy destination, while challenges in infrastructure warrant attention for sustained growth and prosperity.

The Ramechhap district has been divided into 8 local levels and 2 constituencies with effect from the date of 2073 Falgun 27 the Government of Nepal. The center of the Doramba Sailung Rural Municipality (Gaupalika) (दोरम्बा शैलुङ गाउँपालिका, रामेछाप) is Doramba-3, Thamchaur. Doramba Gaupalika is bounded on the north by Dolakha district, on the south by Sindhuli, on the west by Kavrepalanchok, on the east by Okhaldhunga and Solukhumbhu.

Doramba Rural Municipality is located in the northwestern part of the Ramechhap district. It is made up of six VDCs including Savik Daduwa, Doramba, Tokarpur, Goshwara, Lakhanpur, and Gunsi. The geographical location, historical identity, and nomenclature, political location, natural and cultural excellence, development prospects of this rural municipality with hilly features under Bagmati Pradesh are explained in the following headings.

Ramechhap is a Himalayan district located in the Janakpur Zone of Bagmati Pradesh, Nepal. Although close to the capital, it is a remote area in terms of service facilities. Kavrepalanchok district, which is touched by the capital, lies between Dolakha and Okhaldhunga districts bordering China and Sindhuli district, which is touched by the Terai. This district of 1546 sq. Km is neglected despite having sufficient resources. Ramechhap is also known as the district of Tintal. Subba Krishnalal Adhikari, Martyr Ganga Lal Shrestha, and Founder General of the Communist Party of Nepal Pushpalal Shrestha were born in Ramechhap.

Geographical location:
Doramba village, situated at an altitude of 715 m to 3138 m above sea level, is geographically situated at 27 degrees 28 minutes 41 seconds to 27 degrees 36 minutes 52 seconds north latitude and 85 degrees 49 minutes 27 seconds to 86 degrees 1 minutes 30 seconds east longitude. Doramba village municipality is located in the northwestern part of Ramechhap district. It is bounded on the east by Manthali Municipality and Dolakha District, on the west by Kavrepalanchok District, Sunapati Rural Municipality, and Khandadevi Rural Municipality and on the north by Dolakha District. Occupying 8.99 percent of the total area of ​​the district.

Historical Identification and Naming:
Doramba Sailung Rural Municipality is a region with historical, religious, cultural, and natural features. Daduwa, Doramba, Tokarpur, Goshwara, Lakhanpur, and Gunsi VDCs under the former Doramba area. Doramba rural municipality was formed in 2073 BS. This rural municipality is one of the major areas of historical and tourist importance. Agleshwar, Shillong, Sano Shillong, Kantheshwar Temple, and Brahma Vishnu, which are of special religious and historical importance, still exist. Indigenous tribes live in large numbers here. The word Doramba is also associated with the Tamang language and culture of the indigenous tribes. In the Tamang language, do means 'two' and ramba means 'means'. Mane Tamang is a sacred place of worship according to culture. It is believed that Doramba came into being in the sense of two meanings of the Tamangs and later the name of this place became Doramba. This rural municipality seems to have been named after the two sacred places of worship, namely Doramba.

Natural Resources:
Chauri Khola, Ghatte Khola, and Dhobi Khola are the main natural resources of the village. Irrigation services are available from these rivers which are the main source of irrigation in the lands of the lower Vesi region. Pakhanveda, Katuki, Satuva, Vishjada, Chauri, Sheep, Cattle, Buffalo, Goat, Raga, Danphe, Kalij, Deer, Bear, Leopard, Rabbit, Sparrow, Tiger, Crow, Peacock Are in the form. Apart from this, there are forests and meadows in most parts of the upper part of the hill, and minerals including limestone and copper mines are found in this area.

Cultural Excellence:
Magar, Tamang, Sherpa and other indigenous tribes live in this rural municipality is a unique confluence of Hindu culture. Nepali is the main working and spoken language in this rural municipality which has a mixture of indigenous tribes, Chhetri, Brahmin, and Dalit castes.

Dupcheshwor mahadev is one of the famous holy place specially for hindu followers. It has an amazing history for the formation of this temple. Once in a village all the cows of the villagers were suddenly disappeared. People were so worried about the situation. Then they started to search for their cows. While searching they reach deeper in the forest hill. Suddenly one of the villager saw all the cows gathering at one plece. He closely noticed the activities of those cows and saw that they were one by one milking over a big stone lying over there. After seeing this he gathered all the villagers and told them the incident. People thought that it was a kind of miracle and the stone was an symbol of god mahadev originally called 'Shiva Linga'. Then they make a temple over there and started to worship lord Mahadev. Since then it is a very a sacred place for hindus.
Known as the second Pashupati in Bagmati Province, Dupcheswor Mahadev temple is one of the famous temples of Lord Shiva in Nuwakot district. The highly revered temple, which is visited mostly for its religious beliefs, is a natural structure in the middle of big rocks. Thousands of visitors come to worship the temple all along the year but, the temple is crowded mainly during festivals like big Mela on the days of Dhanyapurnima (full moon day in Mangshir or Poush), Shivaratri, Teej, Balachaturdashi, Janaipurnima, etc. Many pilgrims come here and offer cow milk to God.

HISTORY
According to mythology, around 400 years ago, a local Tamang's milking cow was lost. Later, it was found that the cow used to pour its milk over the Shila – a unique stone projection of a cylindrical shape. The same stone now is considered the representation of Lord Shiva. Earlier, it was called 'Dudheshwor Mahadev' while, later, it became known as 'Dupcheswor Mahadev'.

RELIGIOUS BELIEF
The temple is a central belief for the Hindus and Buddhists. Mostly, the religious place is a destination for childless couples. It is believed that on doing some rituals with pure heart and soul, the desire or the wish of having children comes true. It is also said by the priests of the temple. Moreover, some pilgrims even say that dumb kids can speak after praying in the temple. The divine power of the temple is believed, and hence worshippers from different places come here to place their wishes (भाकल), and it comes true, they again visit the temple and offer cow milk to God.

SPECIALTY
A special carnival takes place at Dupcheswor annually on the full moon day of the Nepali month of Mangshir or Poush, called Dhanyapurnima. It is one of the biggest festivals in the entire district. The festival usually starts on the Ekadasi and ends on the Ekadashi. During this time, pilgrims from all over the country, as well as tourists visit this place. The place not only has local cultural importance but is also famous as a tourist destination in the district.

GETTING THERE
The Duspcheswor Mahadev temple is located on the banks of the Suryamati (Tadi) river. It is 60 km north of Kathmandu's Gangabu and 35 km east of Nuwakot's district headquarters of Bidur, Dupcheswor.
It takes 3 hours to reach there from Kathmandu in a private jeep. Likewise, it is a 15-20 mins walk from the Dupcheswor Mahadev bus station.

Wow and wow!! I spent a good couple of hours wandering around the elephant breeding centre while many people whizzed through, taking photographs without really stopping. I am glad I did.

I read reviews where people complained about the elephants being chained. I took the time to find out why, chatting to a couple of the elephant handlers to understand how it operates. They explained that the elephants are free in the jungle for six hours per day, grazing, socialising and eating. They return to the centre each afternoon so they can be protected from poachers and their babies protected from tigers. These families of elephants form part of a government re-wilding program. They do good work.

The mothers look healthy and reasonably happy, interacting with their handlers without any aggression on either side. The babies are playful and content. They are clearly well fed and well loved, their handlers attentive to their needs.

We had an interesting commotion when a wild bull elephant entered the area. Apparently, he has fathered all of the babies and some of the mothers. He has never been in captivity and the handlers were extremely wary of his movements. He has a long history of killing humans, but is left in peace. I was struck by how powerful he was, especially as he was at least 50% larger than the females.

The babies have some training to keep them and their handlers safe, which is understandable for the success of the re-wilding program. It is very clear that there is zero exploitation here.

It is worth spending some time at the elephant breeding centre to see some great initiatives in action.

Gagan Batika, nestled in the quaint area of Nagbahal in Patan, is a hidden gem that offers a serene escape from the bustling urban life of Kathmandu Valley. Despite being situated in the heart of a vibrant city, Gagan Batika exudes a sense of tranquility and peace that is rarely found in such close proximity to urban chaos.

The entrance to Gagan Batika is unassuming, almost like a secret waiting to be discovered. As you step inside, you are greeted by a lush garden adorned with a variety of plants and flowers, creating a natural oasis that instantly calms the senses. The sound of chirping birds and the gentle rustling of leaves replace the usual city noise, providing a soothing backdrop for relaxation and reflection.

One of the most striking features of Gagan Batika is its traditional Newari architecture. The beautifully restored buildings, with their intricately carved wooden windows and doors, showcase the rich cultural heritage of the area. The open courtyards, lined with antique artifacts and traditional decor, invite visitors to pause and admire the craftsmanship that has stood the test of time.

Despite its central location, Gagan Batika feels like a world apart. The peaceful ambiance is enhanced by the presence of meditation and yoga spaces, where one can engage in practices that nurture the mind and soul. The calm environment is perfect for unwinding, reading a book, or simply enjoying a moment of solitude away from the city's hustle and bustle.

Gagan Batika also serves as a cultural hub, hosting various workshops, art exhibitions, and community events. These activities not only promote local talent but also provide a platform for cultural exchange and learning. The sense of community is palpable, with both locals and visitors coming together to celebrate art, culture, and mindfulness.

What makes Gagan Batika truly special is its ability to offer a peaceful retreat without being disconnected from the conveniences of city life. Excellent cafes, local eateries, and shops are just a short walk away, making it an ideal spot for those seeking a balance between tranquility and accessibility.

In conclusion, Gagan Batika is an unfound gem in the middle of a big city, offering a peaceful sanctuary that blends natural beauty, cultural richness, and community spirit. It is a place where time seems to slow down, allowing visitors to experience the quiet joys of life amidst the vibrant urban landscape of Patan. Whether you are a resident or a traveler, a visit to Gagan Batika promises a rejuvenating experience that lingers long after you leave.

Tundal Devi's lost jewelry is annually sought in Gahana Pokhari, situated in Ward No. 5 of Kathmandu Metropolitan City. The quest begins every year during the waxing moon of Chaitra (March-April), starting from Chaturdashi.

The Bhatbhateni Jatra, commencing on Chaitra Shukla Chaturdashi each year, is celebrated grandly in Handigaon (Ward No. 5) and Tundal Devi Baluwatar area (Ward No. 4) of Kathmandu Metropolitan City. During the Jatra, deities are given a ceremonial rest. On Baisakh Krishna Tritiya, the Bhatbhateni women's group performs a special puja as part of the festivities.

The Bhatbhateni Jatra is a significant and distinctive celebration in Kathmandu, also known as Handi Gaon, Tundal Devi, and Jewel Searching Jatra.

As part of the festival, the Bhatbhateni is adorned and taken out of the temple. The origin of this journey is rooted in a story from many years ago when Tundal Devi, along with Mahalakshmi of Naxal, Manmainju of Balaju, and Devi Nuwakoti, went to the site of the present Gahanapokhri for a bath. It is believed that Tundal Devi's jewelry was lost in the pond during this bathing excursion, giving rise to the significance of Gahanapokhri and the tradition of searching for the lost jewels, a practice believed to have commenced from that time.

Galkot Durbar is a historical palace and cultural heritage site located in the Galkot Municipality of Baglung district in Nepal. It was built in the 15th century by King Mukunda Sen of the Sen dynasty and was used as a palace for the rulers of Galkot. The palace complex covers an area of approximately 5.7 hectares and includes several buildings, courtyards, and temples. The palace is known for its unique architectural style and intricate carvings, which reflect the cultural and artistic traditions of the 15th century. Today, Galkot Durbar is a popular tourist destination and a symbol of Nepal's rich cultural heritage.

From majestic waterfowls like ducks and geese to colorful migratory birds such as egrets, herons, and storks, the sanctuary is teeming with avian life throughout the year.

Visiting Ghodaghodi Lake offers a unique opportunity to observe birds in their natural habitat. Whether you're an avid birder or a casual observer, the sight of numerous species flitting about the tranquil waters and lush vegetation is sure to captivate you. The serene atmosphere of the sanctuary adds to the experience, allowing you to immerse yourself in the sights and sounds of nature.

Apart from its rich birdlife, Ghodaghodi Lake also serves as an educational and conservation hub. Local authorities and conservationists work tirelessly to protect the sanctuary and its inhabitants, raising awareness about the importance of preserving wetland ecosystems and biodiversity.

Overall, Ghodaghodi Lake stands as a testament to the beauty and importance of Nepal's natural heritage. As a bird sanctuary, it not only provides a sanctuary for avian species but also offers visitors a glimpse into the wonders of the natural world. Whether you're a bird lover, a nature enthusiast, or simply someone seeking tranquility amidst breathtaking scenery, Ghodaghodi Lake is sure to leave a lasting impression.

The Gosainkunda Trek (6-7 days from Kathmandu) is a breathtaking journey that I would highly recommend to any trekking enthusiast! Gosaikunda is a holy lake that is worshipped by the Hindus and Buddhists of Nepal and Surya Peak is situated in the north of the lake. After you reach at the peak you will be amazed by the beauty of Sarswoti Lake, Bhairab Lake, and the legendary Gosainkunda Lake.
My experience was nothing short of magical, and here’s why:
Stunning Scenery: The trek offers some of the most beautiful landscapes I've ever seen. From lush green hills to rugged mountain paths, every step was filled with awe-inspiring views. The sight of the majestic Langtang range against the backdrop of clear blue skies was a highlight that I will cherish forever.
Challenging Yet Rewarding: The trek is definitely challenging, with steep ascents and descents, especially as you approach Gosainkunda Lake. However, the effort is well worth it! Reaching the lake at an altitude of 4,380 meters felt like an incredible achievement, and the serene beauty of the lake surrounded by snow-capped peaks took my breath away.
Cultural Experience: Along the way, I had the opportunity to interact  with Sherpas and Tamangs who have different culture and you can get a chance to learn in depth about them. Their warmth and hospitality added depth to the experience. I enjoyed traditional meals at the tea houses and learned about their customs and traditions, which made the trek even more enriching.
Well-Marked Trail: The trail is well-marked, making navigation easier, even for those who may not be experienced trekkers. There are plenty of spots to stop and take breaks, and the views just get better the higher you go.
Wildlife and Nature: I was fortunate enough to see a variety of wildlife, including Himalayan monkeys and various bird species. The flora is equally impressive, with vibrant rhododendron forests that burst into color during the spring.
Accommodations: The tea houses along the route were comfortable, with friendly hosts who made me feel right at home. The food was delicious and varied, catering to both local and international tastes.
Final Thoughts: If you’re looking for a trek that combines natural beauty, cultural immersion, and a sense of adventure, the Gosainkunda Trek is the perfect choice. It’s a journey that challenges you physically while rewarding you with unforgettable memories and stunning vistas.  All you need is to be fit and healthy and the willingness and capability of walking for around 7 to 9 hours every day.

Gosaikunda is a sacred alpine lake in Nepal, situated at 4,380 meters within Langtang National Park. Revered by Hindus and Buddhists, it is believed to be the abode of Lord Shiva. Pilgrims visit during Janai Purnima to take a holy dip in its waters. Surrounded by stunning peaks, it’s also a popular trekking destination.

Gosainkunda is a breathtaking alpine lake located at an altitude of 4,380 meters (14,370 feet) in the Langtang National Park, Nepal. It is a serene and spiritually significant destination that attracts both trekkers and pilgrims alike. The lake is surrounded by rugged mountain terrain, making it a truly magical spot for nature lovers and adventure seekers.

The journey to Gosainkunda is as rewarding as the destination itself. The trek passes through lush forests, traditional Tamang villages, and high-altitude landscapes, offering diverse natural beauty. Upon reaching the lake, you are greeted with crystal-clear blue waters set against the backdrop of snow-capped peaks. The reflections on the lake are mesmerizing, especially during sunrise and sunset, creating a truly unforgettable experience.

Gosainkunda holds immense cultural and religious importance for Hindus and Buddhists, who believe the lake was created by Lord Shiva. It is a popular pilgrimage site, especially during the Janai Purnima festival, when thousands of devotees visit to take a holy dip in its sacred waters.

Whether you seek adventure, peace, or spirituality, Gosainkunda offers a perfect blend of natural beauty and cultural significance. It is a must-visit destination for trekkers and travelers exploring Nepal’s Himalayas!

Guheshwari Temple: A Sacred Abode of Divine Power

Located just 1km east of the revered Pashupatinath Temple, on the southern bank of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Nepal, Guheshwari Temple stands as a testament to the profound spiritual heritage of the region.

At the heart of this holy site lies the deity Mahadevi Guhyekali, symbolizing the primordial Aadhi Shakti, or Divine Power. The temple's energy dynamics, intricately linked with its proximity to the Pashupatinath Temple, add to its spiritual significance, drawing devout tantric worshipers seeking divine blessings.

Originally built in the pagoda style, the temple was meticulously renovated in the 17th century by King Pratap Malla, preserving its architectural splendor for generations to come.

Guheshwari Temple comes alive during its main festivals, such as Chaitra Dashain, Bada Dashain, and Navratri, when devotees flock to pay homage to the divine feminine energy embodied within its sacred walls.

Legend intertwines with mythology at Guheshwari Temple, as it is believed to mark the spot where Sati Devi, in her fury at the disrespect shown to her husband Shiva by her father Daksha, immolated herself. Unable to bear her loss, Shiva carried her body, and as her divine form disintegrated, her body parts fell to earth, creating the 51 Shakti Peeths. Guheshwari Temple stands as a testament to this myth, marking the place where Sati Devi's hips fell, infusing the site with the divine power of the universe.

For centuries, Guheshwari Temple has been a focal point of spiritual reverence, drawing pilgrims and seekers from far and wide to bask in its divine aura and connect with the primal energy that permeates its sacred precincts.

I stepped into Bhaktapur Durbar Square, and my breath was taken away. Many visitors to Nepal often skip this heritage site in favor of the stunning mountain vistas, but as a history buff, I was as excited as a kid unwrapping a present.

The intricate carvings resembled an ancient jewelry box that had come to life. Ornate wooden structures soared into the sky, their tiered roofs adorned with gleaming golden finials. Stone statues of gods and kings stood as silent sentinels, their weathered faces hinting at centuries of history. If you could erase the few billboards and mobile shops from your view, you might think you were standing in a medieval city teeming with life. Thanks to the Chinese, the rebuilding of this city after the earthquake has been spectacular.

As I wandered around the square, I couldn’t help but reflect on the rich past of this remarkable place. Bhaktapur was once the glittering capital of the Malla kingdom, a powerful dynasty that ruled the Kathmandu Valley for over 300 years. Founded in the 12th century by King Ananda Malla, the city grew into a vital hub along the ancient trade route between India and Tibet. Subsequent rulers, such as Yaksha Malla and Bhupatindra Malla, continued to expand and embellish Bhaktapur, each leaving their mark through grand building projects and artistic patronage. The towering Nyatapola Deval Temple, with its five-tiered roof, stands as a testament to their vision and craftsmanship.

My family, eager to reach Pokhara, was trailing behind me with indulgent smiles. They patiently bore my explorations on the condition that I would join them in their adventures the next day. Meanwhile, I could easily sit in this old town forever.

These unexplored connections invite us to look deeper into our shared history. They challenge us to question our preconceived notions about cultural boundaries and inspire us to seek out the common threads that bind us.

From the intricate woodwork of Bhaktapur's temples to the similar craftsmanship found in Kerala's palaces, from the vibrant festivals of Nepal to the ritualistic performances of North Kerala, countless stories are waiting to be unraveled.

Bhaleshwar Mahadev Temple on Chandragiri Hill

Located in the Bagmati Province, straddling the districts of Kathmandu and Makwanpur, the Bhaleshwar Mahadev Temple on Chandragiri Hill is a remarkable destination that combines spiritual reverence, natural beauty, and recreational opportunities. Situated at an elevation of 2,551 meters (8,369 feet) above sea level, the temple offers an exceptional viewpoint over the Kathmandu Valley, making it an ideal spot for both sunrise and sunset views.

Scenic Views and Spiritual Significance

One of the most captivating aspects of visiting the Bhaleshwar Mahadev Temple is the awe-inspiring panoramic view of the Kathmandu Valley. The temple’s elevated position provides an unobstructed vista, allowing visitors to take in the sprawling urban landscape below, framed by the majestic Himalayan mountains. Sunrise and sunset are particularly magical times to visit, as the sky transforms into a canvas of vibrant colors, casting a serene glow over the valley and enhancing the spiritual ambiance of the temple.

The Bhaleshwar Mahadev Temple itself is a beautiful and sacred site dedicated to Lord Shiva. It attracts numerous devotees who come to offer prayers and seek blessings. The temple’s architecture, combined with the tranquil surroundings, creates a peaceful environment perfect for meditation and reflection. The spiritual energy of the place, coupled with the natural beauty, makes it a must-visit for those seeking both solace and inspiration.

Adventure and Recreation

Beyond its spiritual and scenic appeal, Chandragiri Hill offers a range of adventurous activities that cater to thrill-seekers. The zipline and cycling paths provide an adrenaline rush against the backdrop of stunning natural scenery. The zipline experience, in particular, offers a unique way to appreciate the landscape, soaring above the treetops with a bird’s-eye view of the surroundings.

For families and individuals looking for more leisurely pursuits, Chandragiri Hill does not disappoint. The area features well-maintained playgrounds and parks that are perfect for children, ensuring they have a fun and engaging experience. Adults can also enjoy these spaces, whether for a relaxing stroll or a picnic. Additionally, horse riding is available, offering a delightful way to explore the hill’s trails and enjoy the fresh mountain air.

Dining and Amenities

After a day of exploration and spiritual enrichment, visitors can enjoy a variety of dining options on Chandragiri Hill. The hilltop is home to several good restaurants that cater to diverse culinary preferences, offering both vegetarian and non-vegetarian cuisine. These establishments provide a comfortable place to rest and refuel while enjoying delicious meals with stunning views as a backdrop.

Conclusion

Bhaleshwar Mahadev Temple on Chandragiri Hill is an exceptional destination that offers a unique blend of spirituality, adventure, and leisure. Its prime location in the Bagmati Province, with easy access from both Kathmandu and Makwanpur, makes it a convenient getaway for locals and tourists alike. Whether you are drawn by the spiritual allure of the temple, the breathtaking views of the Kathmandu Valley, the thrilling adventure activities, or the family-friendly amenities, Chandragiri Hill promises a memorable experience for visitors of all ages.

The Chandragiri Hils are quite significant from a historical standpoint. It was from these hills that King Prithivi Narayan Shah caught the first glimpse of a much scenic and prosperous Kathmandu valley, which in fact instilled in the king's mind an idea of annexing the valley into his kingdom According to folklore, Prithivi Narayan Shah is beleved to have amassed spiritual powers for unification process after undergoing rigorous meditation or 'sadhana' at these very hilis. The Gorkhali king disguised himself while ascending the hills in order to avoid being recognized by the Malla Kings of Kathmandu in his Divine Preaching (Divyopades), it has been mentioned that King Prithivi Narayan was determined to first annex and then make Kathmandu the capital of unified Nepal. He apparently first saw the valley while on his way back to his kingdom in Gorkha from his in-law's realm in Makwanpur According to Historian Prof. Dr. Dinesh Raj Panta, astrologers Bhanu Aryal and Kulananda Dhakal who accompanied the king during that trip had made a prediction that their king's wish to takeover Kathmandu would definitely come true. As per popular belief, pleased with his perseverance and Sadhana, it was Bhaleshwara Mahadev that granted King Prithivi Narayan Shah his wishes

Chitwan National Park is the oldest and most famous national park in Nepal. It is world-renowned for its biodiversity and wildlife. This park is also listed on the World Heritage Site.
Why is Chitwan National Park special?
* One-horned rhinoceros: Chitwan is world famous for the one-horned rhinoceros. Here you can find the largest number of one-horned rhinoceros in the world.
* Wildlife: Along with rhinoceros, there are tigers, deer, leopards, and many other wild animals here.
* Birds: Chitwan is also famous for birds. Hundreds of species of birds can be found here.
* Natural beauty: The rivers, forests, and meadows here reflect the natural beauty.
What to do in Chitwan?
* Jungle safari: You can go on a jungle safari by jeep safari, elephant safari, or on foot.
* Bird watching: Chitwan is an excellent destination for bird watching.
* Boating on the river: You can enjoy the natural scenery by boating on the river.
* Visit Tharu village: You can visit the Tharu village to learn about the lifestyle and culture of the local Tharu community.
How to plan a trip?
* When to go: You can visit Chitwan at any time except during the rainy season.
* Where to stay: There are many types of lodges and hotels available in Chitwan.
* What to bring: Bring necessary clothes, shoes, sunscreen, and insect repellent for jungle safari.
Chitwan National Park is Nepal's natural heritage. A visit here will make a lifetime memory for you.

Benches and open spaces make it family and picnic-friendly.

Informative plaques provide historical context.

Located near Thamel, it’s easy to reach.

Entry fee is reasonable, but slightly higher for foreign visitors.

The temple's architecture is an exquisite blend of traditional Nepali and Mughal styles, with ornate carvings, intricate woodwork, and vibrant colors. The temple complex includes a large courtyard, various smaller shrines, and a sacred pond, which is believed to have healing powers. The Janaki Temple holds immense cultural and religious significance, especially during the annual festivals of Ram Navami and Vivah Panchami, which celebrate the marriage of Lord Rama and Sita. Pilgrims from across Nepal and India flock to the temple to pay homage and seek blessings. The temple is also a symbol of the deep cultural ties between the people of Nepal and India, reflecting the shared heritage of the Ramayana epic.

Inspiring Experience: Durbar Square, Nepal

I had the privilege of visiting Durbar Square in Kathmandu, Nepal, and it was an experience that left me in awe. This ancient palace complex is a testament to Nepal's rich cultural heritage and architectural prowess.

_Historic Significance_

Durbar Square has been the seat of power for the Malla and Shah dynasties, and its history dates back to the 3rd century BC. The square is home to numerous temples, palaces, and shrines, each with its own unique story to tell.

_Architectural Marvel_

The architecture of Durbar Square is a blend of Nepalese, Tibetan, and Indian styles, showcasing the country's rich cultural diversity. The intricate carvings, ornate details, and majestic structures will leave you spellbound.

_Things to Do_

1. _Explore the Palaces_: Visit the ancient palaces, including the Hanuman Dhoka Palace and the Basantapur Palace.
2. _Discover the Temples_: Explore the numerous temples, including the Kumari Temple, the Taleju Temple, and the Bhagwati Temple.
3. _Watch the Ceremonies_: Witness the traditional ceremonies and rituals performed by the locals.
4. _Shop for Souvenirs_: Browse the local shops and stalls selling traditional handicrafts, souvenirs, and street food.

_Tips and Essentials_

1. _Dress Modestly_: Dress conservatively and remove your shoes before entering the temples and palaces.
2. _Respect Local Customs_: Respect the local customs and traditions, and avoid taking pictures during ceremonies.
3. _Hire a Guide_: Hire a local guide to get a deeper understanding of the history and significance of Durbar Square.
4. _Be Prepared for Crowds_: Be prepared for crowds and long lines, especially during peak season.

_In Conclusion_

Durbar Square is a must-visit destination for anyone traveling to Nepal. Its rich history, stunning architecture, and vibrant culture make it an unforgettable experience. Whether you're a history buff, a culture enthusiast, or simply a curious traveler, Durbar Square has something to offer everyone.
